rag.content:
/-- `Pi.algHom` commutes with composition. -/
theorem algHom_comp {B C : Type*} [Semiring B] [Algebra R B] [Semiring C] [Algebra R C]
    (g : ∀ i, C →ₐ[R] A i) (h : B →ₐ[R] C) :
    (algHom R A g).comp h = algHom R A (fun i ↦ (g i).comp h) := rfl

rag.name: Function.algebra
rag.content:
/-- A special case of `Pi.algebra` for non-dependent types. Lean struggles to elaborate
definitions elsewhere in the library without this. -/
instance Function.algebra {R : Type*} (ι : Type*) (A : Type*) [CommSemiring R] [Semiring A]
    [Algebra R A] : Algebra R (ι → A) :=
  Pi.algebra _ _

rag.name: Pi.evalAlgHom
rag.content:
/-- `Function.eval` as an `AlgHom`. The name matches `Pi.evalRingHom`, `Pi.evalMonoidHom`,
etc. -/
@[simps]
def evalAlgHom (i : ι) : (Π i, A i) →ₐ[R] A i :=
  { Pi.evalRingHom A i with
    toFun := fun f ↦ f i
    commutes' := fun _ ↦ rfl }

class SemialgHomClass (F : Type*) {R S : outParam Type*}
  [CommSemiring R] [CommSemiring S] (φ : outParam (R →+* S)) (A B : outParam Type*)

rag.name: Pi.algHom
rag.content:
/-- A family of algebra homomorphisms `g i : B →ₐ[R] A i` defines a ring homomorphism
`Pi.algHom g : B →ₐ[R] Π i, A i` given by `Pi.algHom g x i = g i x`. -/
@[simps!]
def algHom {B : Type*} [Semiring B] [Algebra R B] (g : ∀ i, B →ₐ[R] A i) : B →ₐ[R] Π i, A i where
  __ := Pi.ringHom fun i ↦ (g i).toRingHom
  commutes' r := by ext; simp

informal_statement:
For any product type \( \Pi \) and given semialgebra homomorphisms \( g_i : A \to f(i) \) in the context of a commutative semiring \( S \), the application of the semialgebra homomorphism \( \text{Pi.semiAlgHom} \) to an element \( a \) of \( A \) and an index \( i \) is equal to applying the \( i \)-th component function \( g_i \) to \( a \). In other words, for any \( a \) in \( A \) and \( i \) in \( I \), we have:

\[
(\text{Pi.semiAlgHom}\, \phi\, g)\, a\, i = g\, i\, a
\]

This equality holds definitionally, meaning both sides are the same by the way they are constructed.

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a
